before:
A journey can trust the headers on a request the routing service forwards. No journey frontend has a public URL, so a request from the internet reaches a journey only through the routing service, and only the routing service can set the prefix and session headers that request carries.

A journey can only trust those headers up to the platform boundary: services inside CDP can reach journey URLs directly and supply their own session and `X-Forwarded-Prefix` headers. Journey frontends redirect direct requests to the INS hostname, using the request's `Host` and absence of a forwarded prefix to identify them. The redirect handles stray links and misconfiguration, but cannot authenticate a caller inside CDP that can set those headers. How journeys validate those internal requests is a decision rather than a gap: CDP recommends service tokens, and a receiver validates the token then pins the caller by its subject. INS has still to decide which routes must carry a token, and which receivers pin a named caller.
after:
For a request from the internet, a journey can trust the headers forwarded by the routing service. No journey frontend has a public URL, so the request reaches the journey only through the routing service. Only the routing service can set the prefix and session headers that request carries.

This trust ends at the platform boundary. Services inside CDP can reach journey URLs directly and supply their own session and `X-Forwarded-Prefix` headers.

Journey frontends identify direct requests using the request's `Host` and the absence of a forwarded prefix, then redirect them to the INS hostname. This handles stray links and misconfiguration. It cannot authenticate a caller inside CDP that can set those headers.

For internal requests, CDP recommends service tokens: a receiver validates the token, then pins the caller by its subject. INS still has to decide which routes must carry a token and which receivers pin a named caller.

before: INS proposes to audit the events that establish or change who can act, and the events in which someone exercises that access: sign-in and sign-out outcomes, session creation and session end, organisation switches, every action taken for another organisation, and B2B user access to notifications and files. Each event names the acting user by the subject from the verified token, the organisation context, the outcome, and the artefact when the event concerns one. No audit event carries the sealed session token or the session identifier.

Sign-in is unchanged in substance. The front door remains the only component that talks to an identity provider, the same three bindings tie the callback, the assertion and the code to the request INS started, the same checks run on the assertion before any session exists, the return path is checked against the route allowlist, and a script call without a session receives an unauthenticated status rather than a redirect. Users are identified by issuer and subject together in both designs. The proposal leaves both lifetime values open for product and security to declare and gives eight hours only as an illustration; this comparison uses thirty minutes of inactivity and an eight-hour absolute end as working values for both designs, and every window quoted in this document hangs off those two numbers. Both designs judge expiry at the moment a request arrives rather than by any housekeeping. The cookie design also allows for clock error, in three thirty-second steps: a front-door instance may run thirty seconds fast, a consumer treats a timestamp as reached only thirty seconds after the stamp, and the consumer's own clock may run thirty seconds slow. Every nominal window in this document therefore widens by up to a minute and a half at the far end: thirty minutes past the last contact becomes about thirty-one and a half, fifty past the last authentication about fifty-two, and the eight-hour end about eight hours and one and a half minutes. The session-service design's own absolute end is a formula with an open operand, the lesser of the provider's renewal window and a limit INS declares, and the renewal window is itself unsettled between the twenty-four hours the provider's onboarding guide records and a fourteen-day platform default, so that design's declared end is not yet a number either.

before: Ending a session for lost access changes character. The session-service design ends on the provider's explicit refusal to renew. The cookie design never asks the provider to renew; it asks for a fresh authorisation with the relationship pre-selected, the exchange succeeds, and INS infers a verdict from what the assertion contains: a different relationship, no approved role where the cookie carried one, or an explicit denial. That is a weaker signal, since INS rather than the provider is now judging, and it reaches INS only at the next reauthentication, within twenty minutes plus one navigation for a navigating user and at most fifty minutes for anyone. Two cases are kept apart from a refusal so that the inference does not sign out the wrong people. An assertion with no roles claim at all is retried once with the picker forced rather than read as a refusal, because a rule treating an absent claim as a refusal would clear every session in the service twenty minutes after sign-in. And a user who legitimately holds no role, an ordinary state while an organisation's administrator has yet to assign one, keeps their session and is denied by default rather than being signed out every twenty minutes. It also rests on the provider re-evaluating the user's roles when it issues that assertion rather than replaying the roles it established when the picker last ran in that session. The provider is confirmed to re-evaluate on the refresh path, which is the path the cookie design discards, and confirmed for nothing else. If the roles are replayed, a lost role goes undetected until the provider's own session lapses, which for a continuously active user may be the whole eight hours. Bounding it would then mean forcing the picker at each reauthentication, which shows every multi-organisation user a screen every interval. So a bounded staleness is achievable either silently or at the cost of a screen, and which of the two is not known until the provider's behaviour is observed.
after:
Ending a session after access is lost works differently in the two designs. The session-service design ends the session when the provider explicitly refuses to renew the session.

The cookie design never asks the provider to renew. It asks for a fresh authorisation with the relationship pre-selected. The exchange succeeds, and INS infers a verdict from what the assertion contains:

- a different relationship;
- no approved role where the cookie carried one; or
- an explicit denial.

This is a weaker signal because INS, rather than the provider, judges the assertion. It reaches INS only at the next reauthentication: within twenty minutes plus one navigation for a navigating user, and at most fifty minutes for anyone.

Two cases must not be treated as refusals. An assertion with no roles claim at all is retried once with the picker forced. Treating an absent claim as a refusal would clear every session in the service twenty minutes after sign-in. A user who legitimately has no role, an ordinary state while an organisation's administrator has yet to assign one, keeps their session and is denied by default instead of being signed out every twenty minutes.

The role-staleness bound also depends on the provider re-evaluating the user's roles when it issues that assertion rather than replaying the roles it established when the picker last ran in that session. The provider is confirmed to re-evaluate on the refresh path, which the cookie design discards, and confirmed for nothing else. If the roles are replayed, a lost role goes undetected until the provider's own session lapses. For a continuously active user, that may be the whole eight hours.

Bounding the staleness would mean forcing the picker at each reauthentication. That shows every multi-organisation user a screen every interval. Bounded staleness is therefore achievable either silently or at the cost of a screen. Which outcome applies remains unknown until the provider's behaviour is observed.
